title: DOJ Refuses to Rule Out Intervening in Election Certification Under 'Doomsday' Scenarios
snippet: Attorney General Todd Blanche acknowledged hypothetical scenarios where the Department of Justice might block election certification, amid escalating legal clashes over federal election monitoring and voter roll purges.
content:
WASHINGTON — Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to completely rule out federal intervention in state election processes on Thursday, acknowledging that extreme, hypothetical "doomsday scenarios" could theoretically prompt the Department of Justice to block the certification of votes.

Speaking with reporters, Blanche insisted that the agency has no intention of meddling in state affairs, but demurred on making blanket promises regarding future developments. "I don't think it's proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what's going to happen in the future, because I have no idea what's happening in the future," Blanche said. He emphasized, however, that he is not structuring his daily schedule around disrupting state certifications, maintaining that the department has no desire to improperly interfere.

Federal Oversight Sparks Democratic Lawsuit

The DOJ previously announced plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors across polling locations nationwide on Election Day. While Blanche framed the deployment as a routine measure to enforce federal voting laws dating back to the 1960s, Democratic leadership and voting rights groups view the move with deep skepticism.

On Tuesday, Democratic groups filed a lawsuit against President Donald Trump and the Department of Justice, alleging widespread voter intimidation and unlawful threats aimed at state election workers. The legal challenge highlights the administration's aggressive efforts to force states to audit voter rolls and remove alleged noncitizens under threat of criminal prosecution.

Clash Over California Voter Rolls

The tension has boiled over sharply in California, where federal prosecutors recently sued state officials for failing to cross-reference voter rolls against a Department of Homeland Security list of 20,000 suspected noncitizens within a 48-hour window. California Governor Gavin Newsom blasted the federal lawsuit, stating firmly that the state's elections "are NOT Donald Trump's to control."

Despite the backlash, the DOJ announced federal charges against 28 alleged non-U.S. citizens in California for illegal voting, claiming each individual appeared on the DHS list provided to the state. Justice Department officials maintain that verifying voter eligibility is a mandate under federal law, while critics argue the administration is amplifying unproven claims of mass noncitizen voting to pressure election authorities.
